**Conventions and definitions.**

Throughout, $X$ is a set and $\mathcal P(X)$ is its power set. For a cardinal $k$ (identified with the set of ordinals below it, so $0=\varnothing$, $1=\{0\}$, $\aleph_0=\mathbb N$), $\mathcal P(X)^k$ is the set of all families $(A_j)_{j<k}$ with each $A_j\in\mathcal P(X)$. In particular $\mathcal P(X)^0=\{()\}$ has exactly one element, the empty family.

*Magma of sets.* Let $(\phi_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of mappings $\phi_i:\mathcal P(X)^{k_i}\to\mathcal P(X)$, where each $k_i$ is a cardinal. A collection $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ is a *magma of sets for $(\phi_i)_{i\in I}$ on $X$* iff for every $i\in I$ and every family $(S_j)_{j<k_i}\in\mathcal S^{k_i}$ we have $\phi_i\big((S_j)_{j<k_i}\big)\in\mathcal S$. (That is, $\mathcal S$ is closed under each operation $\phi_i$.)

*$\sigma$-algebra.* A collection $\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ is a *$\sigma$-algebra on $X$* iff
- (SA1) $X\in\Sigma$;
- (SA2) for all $A\in\Sigma$: $X\setminus A\in\Sigma$;
- (SA3) for every sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$: $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\Sigma$.

**Claim.** Define three operations on $\mathcal P(X)$:
1. $\phi_1:\mathcal P(X)^0\to\mathcal P(X)$, $\phi_1(())=X$ (arity $k_1=0$);
2. $\phi_2:\mathcal P(X)^1\to\mathcal P(X)$, $\phi_2(A)=X\setminus A$ (arity $k_2=1$);
3. $\phi_3:\mathcal P(X)^{\aleph_0}\to\mathcal P(X)$, $\phi_3\big((A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\big)=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n$ (arity $k_3=\aleph_0$).

Then for every $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$: $\mathcal S$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ if and only if $\mathcal S$ is a magma of sets for $(\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3)$ on $X$. Hence the notion of $\sigma$-algebra is an instance of the notion of magma of sets.

**Proof.**

*Step 0: the $\phi_i$ are well-defined mappings into $\mathcal P(X)$.*
- $\phi_1$: its domain $\mathcal P(X)^0=\{()\}$ is a singleton, and its value $X$ satisfies $X\subseteq X$, so $X\in\mathcal P(X)$.
- $\phi_2$: for $A\in\mathcal P(X)$, $X\setminus A\subseteq X$, so $X\setminus A\in\mathcal P(X)$.
- $\phi_3$: for a sequence $(A_n)$ with each $A_n\subseteq X$, every $x\in\bigcup_n A_n$ lies in some $A_n\subseteq X$, so $\bigcup_nA_n\subseteq X$, i.e. $\bigcup_nA_n\in\mathcal P(X)$.

So $(\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3)$ is a legitimate family of operations on $\mathcal P(X)$ of arities $0,1,\aleph_0$.

*Step 1: unpack the magma condition for each operation.* Fix $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$.

(a) Closure under $\phi_1$ means: for every $(S_j)_{j<0}\in\mathcal S^0$, $\phi_1((S_j))\in\mathcal S$. Now $\mathcal S^0=\{()\}$ (there is exactly one family indexed by the empty set, regardless of $\mathcal S$), so this condition says exactly $\phi_1(())\in\mathcal S$, i.e. $X\in\mathcal S$. Thus closure under $\phi_1$ $\iff$ (SA1).

(b) Closure under $\phi_2$ means: for every $(S_0)\in\mathcal S^1$, $\phi_2(S_0)\in\mathcal S$. Families indexed by $1=\{0\}$ with values in $\mathcal S$ correspond bijectively to elements $A=S_0\in\mathcal S$, so the condition says: for all $A\in\mathcal S$, $X\setminus A\in\mathcal S$. Thus closure under $\phi_2$ $\iff$ (SA2).

(c) Closure under $\phi_3$ means: for every $(S_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\in\mathcal S^{\aleph_0}$, $\bigcup_n S_n\in\mathcal S$. The elements of $\mathcal S^{\aleph_0}$ are precisely the sequences $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of members of $\mathcal S$. Thus closure under $\phi_3$ $\iff$ (SA3).

*Step 2: conclude.* By definition, $\mathcal S$ is a magma of sets for $(\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3)$ iff it is closed under $\phi_1$, under $\phi_2$ and under $\phi_3$. By Step 1(a),(b),(c) this holds iff (SA1), (SA2) and (SA3) all hold, i.e. iff $\mathcal S$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$.

($\Rightarrow$) explicitly: if $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra, then $X\in\Sigma$ gives closure under $\phi_1$; (SA2) gives $\phi_2(A)\in\Sigma$ for every $A\in\Sigma$; (SA3) gives $\phi_3((A_n))\in\Sigma$ for every sequence in $\Sigma$. So $\Sigma$ is a magma of sets for $(\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3)$.

($\Leftarrow$) explicitly: if $\mathcal S$ is a magma of sets for $(\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3)$, applying the magma condition to the unique element $()$ of $\mathcal S^0$ gives $X=\phi_1(())\in\mathcal S$; applying it to $A\in\mathcal S$ (as a 1-family) gives $X\setminus A\in\mathcal S$; applying it to any sequence $(A_n)$ in $\mathcal S$ gives $\bigcup_nA_n\in\mathcal S$. So $\mathcal S$ is a $\sigma$-algebra. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks.**
1. *Variant definitions of $\sigma$-algebra.* Some authors replace (SA1) by "$\varnothing\in\Sigma$". Given (SA2), these are equivalent: $\varnothing=X\setminus X$ and $X=X\setminus\varnothing$. For that variant simply use the $0$-ary operation $\phi_1'(())=\varnothing$ instead; the same proof applies verbatim. Others require only "$\Sigma\neq\varnothing$"; under (SA2),(SA3) this is again equivalent to $X\in\Sigma$ (if $A\in\Sigma$, then $X\setminus A\in\Sigma$ and $X=\bigcup_n B_n$ with $B_0=A$, $B_n=X\setminus A$ for $n\ge1$), and the description via $\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3$ above still characterizes exactly these collections.
2. *Role of infinitary arity.* The magma-of-sets framework permits operations of arbitrary cardinal arity $k_i$; the arity $\aleph_0$ of $\phi_3$ is essential, since countable unions are not in general obtainable from finitely many finitary operations. The $0$-ary operation $\phi_1$ encodes the requirement that a distinguished set belongs to the collection; note that this closure condition is non-vacuous precisely because $\mathcal S^0$ is nonempty (it is $\{()\}$) even when $\mathcal S=\varnothing$, which is why the empty collection is correctly excluded from being a $\sigma$-algebra.
